title: Internet Message Access Protocol - Version 4rev1
summary: Defines IMAP4rev1, which lets a client access and manipulate email on a server. It allows mailboxes to be handled as if local, supports offline resynchronization, and includes operations to create, delete and rename mailboxes and check for new messages. It was replaced by RFC 9051.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet Message Access Protocol version 4 revision 1 (IMAP4rev1) lets a mail client manage messages stored on a server. It supports mailbox operations, searches and resynchronization after offline use.

questions: what is the difference between imap uid and sequence number
subtitle: The protocol for reading, organizing and searching mail stored on a server.

tldr.problem: A mail client needs to access messages and mailbox information stored on a server, including after the client has been offline.
tldr.mechanism: IMAP4rev1 uses tagged commands and server responses to manage mailboxes, messages, flags, searches and selective message retrieval over a reliable stream such as TCP.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3501 was obsoleted by RFC 9051 and was updated by the RFCs listed in the supplied metadata.

today: RFC 3501 was obsoleted by RFC 9051. The supplied metadata also lists later RFCs that updated RFC 3501.

sections.title: What IMAP4rev1 Provides
sections.content:
IMAP4rev1 lets a client access and manipulate messages on a server and work with remote mailboxes much like local folders. It includes commands to create, delete and rename mailboxes; search; change flags; remove messages; and fetch selected message data.

The protocol supports offline clients that resynchronize with the server. It supports one server and does not specify how to post mail; the RFC points to mail-transfer protocols for that task.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can use IMAP to manage mailboxes and messages held on a server. It can also reconnect after offline use and synchronize its view with the server.

sections.title: Commands, Tags and Responses
sections.content:
IMAP4rev1 assumes a reliable data stream such as TCP; an IMAP server using TCP listens on port 143. A client begins each command with a tag, and the server uses that tag in the completion response.

The server can send untagged data beginning with an asterisk and can ask the client to continue a command with a plus sign. A tagged OK means success, NO means failure, and BAD reports a protocol error. Clients must be ready to receive server responses at any time.
sections.plainLanguage: Each client command has a tag that the server repeats when it reports the result. The server can also send data or request more command text before completing the command.

sections.title: The Four Connection States
sections.content:
An IMAP connection is in one of four states: not authenticated, authenticated, selected or logout. A normal greeting starts in the not-authenticated state; a pre-authenticated greeting starts in the authenticated state.

After authentication, the client selects a mailbox to enter the selected state. Closing or failing to select a mailbox returns the connection to the authenticated state; logout or connection termination enters the logout state.
sections.plainLanguage: The connection starts before authentication, then enters an authenticated state. The client selects a mailbox before working with its messages and ends the connection by logging out.

sections.title: Message Numbers and Flags
sections.content:
A message can be identified by a message sequence number or a unique identifier (UID). Sequence numbers show a message's current position and can change after a message is expunged; UIDs are 32-bit values assigned in ascending order and are intended to persist between sessions.

Each mailbox has a UIDVALIDITY value used with a UID to identify messages across sessions. Message flags record states such as seen, answered, flagged, deleted or draft; marking a message deleted does not remove it until an EXPUNGE or CLOSE operation.
sections.plainLanguage: A message's position number can change. Its unique identifier is meant to stay stable, while flags record states such as read or deleted.

sections.title: Protecting Mail and Credentials
sections.content:
IMAP4rev1 traffic, including mail, is sent in cleartext unless the connection negotiates STARTTLS, privacy protection through AUTHENTICATE, or another protection mechanism. The LOGIN command sends passwords in cleartext.

The RFC requires servers to be configurable so authentication either uses a protected connection or disables plaintext authentication. During TLS negotiation, the client MUST compare the server name it used with the identity in the server certificate to reduce the risk of a man-in-the-middle attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Without protection, someone monitoring the connection can read mail and passwords. Clients must check the server certificate on an encrypted connection, and servers should limit repeated failed login attempts.
